demo_steps.title: The tetrahedron in 3D
demo_steps.narration: The tetrahedron has vertices at (1,0,0), (0,2,0), and (0,0,4). The slanted face is z = 4−4x−2y. The base region R lies in the xy-plane. Only the slanted face and base are shaded; the coordinate-plane faces are shown as thin edges.

demo_steps.title: Sweep the integration strip
demo_steps.narration: Drag x₀ toward 0: the strip lengthens to y=2 and the curtain reaches z=4. Drag toward 1: both shrink to zero. The curtain height at each point equals 4−4x−2y, the integrand of the volume integral.

demo_steps.title: Project down to the 2D base
demo_steps.narration: Toggle to the 2D view: the tetrahedron collapses to its footprint. The triangle R has vertices (0,0), (1,0), (0,2) with hypotenuse y = 2−2x. The red strip shows the inner integration limits from y=0 to y=2−2x₀. This is exactly the region over which ∫∫(4−4x−2y) dA is evaluated.

demo_steps.title: Strip at the boundary
demo_steps.narration: At x₀ near 1, the strip shrinks to a point — the outer integral's upper limit. At x₀=0, the strip spans the full height y=2. The outer integral runs x from 0 to 1.

plan.geometry_notes: CRITICAL AXIS CONVENTION: z-axis is VERTICAL (screen-up), y-axis points to screen-right, x-axis points toward viewer's lower-left. This matches the source figure's left panel. World units equal coordinate values: x ∈ [0,1] (axis drawn to ~1.2), y ∈ [0,2] (axis to ~2.4), z ∈ [0,4] (axis to ~4.5). Tetrahedron vertices: O=(0,0,0), A=(1,0,0), B=(0,2,0), C=(0,0,4). Slanted plane: z = 4−4x−2y passes through A, B, C. Base R: triangle O,A,B at z=0. FACES: slanted face and base R get semi-transparent fill (teal, opacity 0.45). The xz-plane face (O,A,C) and yz-plane face (O,B,C) are drawn as thin edge lines ONLY — no fill, matching the source. Red strip at x=x₀: vertical line in xy-plane from (x₀,0,0) to (x₀,2−2x₀,0). Curtain quad: vertices (x₀,0,0), (x₀,2−2x₀,0), (x₀,2−2x₀,0), (x₀,0,4−4x₀) — a vertical quad whose top edge lies on the slanted plane. Cross-section line on plane: from (x₀,0,4−4x₀) to (x₀,2−2x₀,0). 2D VIEW (separate scene/camera): true top-down orthographic looking down the z-axis. Show ONLY the xy-plane content: x-axis horizontal (screen-right) from 0 to 1.2, y-axis vertical (screen-up) from 0 to 2.4, tick marks at 0 and 1 on x-axis, at 0 and 2 on y-axis. Triangle R filled light teal. Hypotenuse bold teal labeled 'y = 2−2x'. Red strip at same x₀ position. NO z-axis, NO 3D elements visible. Palette: faces light teal #b8e0dc (opacity 0.45), base R #8fd4cd (opacity 0.55), edges/hypotenuse bold teal #0e9e96, vertex dots #0e9e96, axes black #222, labels black, red strip #cc2222, curtain #e0552a (opacity 0.3), cross-section #e0552a.
plan.notes: Use two separate camera setups toggled by viewMode: (1) 3D axonometric camera with up-vector = +Z, positioned to give the standard math-textbook view (z up, y right, x lower-left); (2) 2D orthographic camera looking straight down −Z with up = +Y, showing only the base-plane elements. Keep both sets of geometry in the scene; toggle visibility groups rather than rebuilding. For the 3D view, render xz and yz faces as THREE.LineSegments (edges only, no mesh fill). The slanted face and base R use THREE.Mesh with transparent DoubleSide material. Recompute curtain quad (4 vertices) and cross-section line (2 points) on every stripX change. For the 2D view, hide all 3D-specific elements (slanted face, curtain, cross-section, z-axis, vertex dots at z>0) and show the flat 2D triangle with proper axis ticks. The transition between views can be a quick fade (200ms) rather than a camera animation, to emphasize these are two distinct representations.

authoredPrompt: This figure is part of a worked example asking to find the volume of the tetrahedron bounded by the coordinate planes and the plane z = 4 - 4x - 2y using a double integral. The figure contains two linked diagrams. Left: a 3D perspective showing the tetrahedron in xyz-space with vertices at (0, 0, 4), (1, 0, 0), and (0, 2, 0), bounded above by the plane z = 4 - 4x - 2y (labeled on the slanted face) with the base region R labeled. Right (inset): the 2D base region R in the xy-plane, a right triangle with vertices at (0, 0), (1, 0), and (0, 2), bounded by the x-axis, y-axis, and the line y = 2 - 2x; a red vertical strip illustrates the inner integration limits from y = 0 to y = 2 - 2x. An arrow connects the two diagrams. The figure establishes the correspondence between the 3D tetrahedron and the triangular base R over which the iterated double integral is set up.
authoredInteractions:
- Drag the red vertical integration strip in the 2D base panel and watch the corresponding cross-section highlight on the 3D plane z=4-4x-2y update in real time
- Rotate the 3D tetrahedron to view the triangular plane from different angles
- Toggle between the 3D and 2D panels to trace how the triangular integration region R projects onto the xy-plane
authoredContext: Use a double integral to find the volume of the tetrahedron bounded by the coordinate planes and the plane z = 4 − 4x − 2y. Solution. The tetrahedron in question is bounded above by the plane z = 4 − 4x − 2y (5) and below by the triangular region R shown in Figure 14.2.10. Thus, the volume is given by V = !! R (4 − 4x − 2y) dA The region R is bounded by the x-axis, the y-axis, and the line y = 2 − 2x [set z = 0 in (5)], so that treating R as a type I region yields V = !! R (4 − 4x − 2y) dA = ! 1 0 ! 2−2x 0 (4 − 4x − 2y) dy dx = ! 1 0 _x001d_ 4y − 4xy − y2_x001e_2−2x y=0 dx = ! 1 0 (4 − 8x + 4x2 )dx = 4

demo_steps.title: 3D solid and a mid strip
demo_steps.narration: The tetrahedron with vertices (1,0,0),(0,2,0),(0,0,4) sits above base R. At x = 0.5 the red strip runs from y = 0 to y = 2 - 2(0.5) = 1, and the orange cross-section on the plane spans z from 4 - 4(0.5) = 2 down to 0.

interactions.label: View
interactions.teaches: Switching between the 3D solid and its 2D footprint reveals how the slanted plane z = 4−4x−2y projects down to the triangular region R, establishing the domain of integration for the double integral

interactions.label: Strip position x₀
interactions.teaches: Sweeping x₀ moves the red inner-integration strip across R; the strip's top endpoint slides along y = 2−2x and the curtain height on the slanted plane changes, showing the inner limits y: 0 → 2−2x and the integrand value at each x
Rotating the 3D view lets the learner confirm the tetrahedron is bounded by three coordinate planes and the slanted plane, and see the curtain cross-section from different angles

demo_steps.title: The tetrahedron in 3D
demo_steps.narration: The tetrahedron has vertices at (1,0,0), (0,2,0), and (0,0,4). The slanted face is z = 4−4x−2y. The base region R lies in the xy-plane. Only the slanted face and base are shaded; the coordinate-plane faces are shown as thin edges.

demo_steps.title: Sweep the integration strip
demo_steps.narration: Drag x₀ toward 0: the strip lengthens to y=2 and the curtain reaches z=4. Drag toward 1: both shrink to zero. The curtain height at each point equals 4−4x−2y, the integrand of the volume integral.

demo_steps.title: Project down to the 2D base
demo_steps.narration: Toggle to the 2D view: the tetrahedron collapses to its footprint. The triangle R has vertices (0,0), (1,0), (0,2) with hypotenuse y = 2−2x. The red strip shows the inner integration limits from y=0 to y=2−2x₀. This is exactly the region over which ∫∫(4−4x−2y) dA is evaluated.

demo_steps.title: Strip at the boundary
demo_steps.narration: At x₀ near 1, the strip shrinks to a point — the outer integral's upper limit. At x₀=0, the strip spans the full height y=2. The outer integral runs x from 0 to 1.

plan.geometry_notes: CRITICAL AXIS CONVENTION: z-axis is VERTICAL (screen-up), y-axis points to screen-right, x-axis points toward viewer's lower-left. This matches the source figure's left panel. World units equal coordinate values: x ∈ [0,1] (axis drawn to ~1.2), y ∈ [0,2] (axis to ~2.4), z ∈ [0,4] (axis to ~4.5). Tetrahedron vertices: O=(0,0,0), A=(1,0,0), B=(0,2,0), C=(0,0,4). Slanted plane: z = 4−4x−2y passes through A, B, C. Base R: triangle O,A,B at z=0. FACES: slanted face and base R get semi-transparent fill (teal, opacity 0.45). The xz-plane face (O,A,C) and yz-plane face (O,B,C) are drawn as thin edge lines ONLY — no fill, matching the source. Red strip at x=x₀: vertical line in xy-plane from (x₀,0,0) to (x₀,2−2x₀,0). Curtain quad: vertices (x₀,0,0), (x₀,2−2x₀,0), (x₀,2−2x₀,0), (x₀,0,4−4x₀) — a vertical quad whose top edge lies on the slanted plane. Cross-section line on plane: from (x₀,0,4−4x₀) to (x₀,2−2x₀,0). 2D VIEW (separate scene/camera): true top-down orthographic looking down the z-axis. Show ONLY the xy-plane content: x-axis horizontal (screen-right) from 0 to 1.2, y-axis vertical (screen-up) from 0 to 2.4, tick marks at 0 and 1 on x-axis, at 0 and 2 on y-axis. Triangle R filled light teal. Hypotenuse bold teal labeled 'y = 2−2x'. Red strip at same x₀ position. NO z-axis, NO 3D elements visible. Palette: faces light teal #b8e0dc (opacity 0.45), base R #8fd4cd (opacity 0.55), edges/hypotenuse bold teal #0e9e96, vertex dots #0e9e96, axes black #222, labels black, red strip #cc2222, curtain #e0552a (opacity 0.3), cross-section #e0552a.
plan.notes: Use two separate camera setups toggled by viewMode: (1) 3D axonometric camera with up-vector = +Z, positioned to give the standard math-textbook view (z up, y right, x lower-left); (2) 2D orthographic camera looking straight down −Z with up = +Y, showing only the base-plane elements. Keep both sets of geometry in the scene; toggle visibility groups rather than rebuilding. For the 3D view, render xz and yz faces as THREE.LineSegments (edges only, no mesh fill). The slanted face and base R use THREE.Mesh with transparent DoubleSide material. Recompute curtain quad (4 vertices) and cross-section line (2 points) on every stripX change. For the 2D view, hide all 3D-specific elements (slanted face, curtain, cross-section, z-axis, vertex dots at z>0) and show the flat 2D triangle with proper axis ticks. The transition between views can be a quick fade (200ms) rather than a camera animation, to emphasize these are two distinct representations.
